course_name: Introduction to Latina and Latino Studies: Movements

course_info.course_name: Introduction to Latina and Latino Studies: Movements

course_details.Overview of class: This course examines formations of various histories and communities through physical and social movements across, and often despite, US geopolitical boundaries. The course explores how the trans-border circulation of peoples and cultures across the Americas influences the development of Latinx socio-spatial relations, intersectional identities, and politics. Additionally, it discusses the broader meanings of these dynamics for critical debates regarding democracy.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
In LATINO 202, by engaging the course materials and one another in discussion and group work, as well as through writing assignments, students will:
1. Understand and explain the historical circumstances of migrations — whether through the shifting of borders or border crossings — that shaped or made Latinx communities.
2. Recognize the particularities of Latinx identity or subjectivity formations across variant regions or urban areas.
3. Discuss and analyze the long history of Latinx social movements, the contexts in which they took shape, and their effects on communities, identities, and politics.
4. Reflect on how Latinxs used formal politics to petition for belated inclusion and civil rights under the law, as well as how and why some Latinxs became skeptical of formal politics (liberal humanism and/or reform), prompting them to begin to imagine, if not deploy, alternatives.)

course_name: Key Concepts and Approaches in Latinx Studies

course_info.course_name: Key Concepts and Approaches in Latinx Studies

course_details.Overview of class:
In this course, students will examine and assess a set of key concepts and approaches in the interdisciplinary field of Latinx Studies, including but not limited to transnationalism, place-making, sanctuary, and Latinidades. Students will further consider historical and contemporary debates and contestations of how these terms and frameworks have shaped the development of the field and thinking about race, class, age, citizenship, gender, and sexuality, among other constructs of social difference.

Take note that students enrolled in this course are required to attend events related to the Block Museum Exhibition: "Pasados Presentes."
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Through a broad range of readings and other course materials and mini-lectures,
students will demonstrate knowledge and understanding oftheoretical and
methodological proposals applied in Latinx Studies and in contributing historical, literary, and social science disciplinary fields.

• Students will also become familiar with and engage academic and popular debates
about the state and direction of Latinx Studies in written assignments, group work and group projects, and by preparing for and participating in classroom discussions.

• Writing assignments and other in-class individual and group exercises and group projects will help students further develop the skills of synthesis, analysis, and dialogue.

course_details.Overview of class:
In the United States, we often talk about Latinx people using blurry labels. We discuss the Latino vote, the Hispanic population, and the Latinx community. This course explores the nuances of these labels through the stories that Latinx authors have been narrating for the past six decades. As we follow characters through conflicts and inhabit their quotidian lives, we will navigate between the specificity of a story and the complexity of a Latinx identity. Class discussions will study emotional ties to places and languages, feminist thought, and the racial and ethnic diversity within the Latinx community. We will read authors such as Gloria Anzaldúa, Justin Torres, Helena Maria Viramontes, and Yxta Maya Murray.

A one-quarter course cannot do justice to the rich genealogy of Latinx writing. This course follows an illustrative sample of authors from the 1970s onward and focuses on short stories, poetry, and essays. It aims to provide students with a historical, political, and literary foundation for further exploration of Latinx literature.

course_details.Overview of class:
The surge in the Latino/a population has brought about profound economic, educational, and political implications for states, cities and the U.S. polity. As their electoral clout continues to grow, as evidenced by recent elections, Latinos/as will have the opportunity to exert greater influence in the politics and policies of our country.

This course will explore these implications and the histories, including the more contemporary social and political developments of Latino communities, in the United States from a comparative framework. We will focus on the political experiences of America's three largest groups of Latino-origin: Mexican Americans, Puerto Ricans, and Cuban Americans.

The first part of the course will examine the social construction of Latino identities and trace the historical experiences of all three groups, comparing the elements behind each group's migration and how those processes affect their incorporation in mainstream society. We also examine demographic resources and the impact of immigration on the politics of the Latino collective. Next, we turn to the development of a Latino politics, placing special emphasis on political attitudes, mobilization strategies and electoral participation. Lastly, we tackle public policy issues such as voting rights and language policy.

The question that we will return to throughout the course is the degree to which and under what circumstances it is appropriate to speak of a Latino community.

course_details.Overview of class: How can desire, creativity, and connection to our bodies serve as catalysts to challenge systems of power? And how and when do joy and pleasure become acts of defiance, opening new possibilities for social transformation? In this course, we will explore the erotic as a source of knowledge and creative power and the capacity it holds for dismantling intersecting systems of oppression in our everyday lives, collectively and individually. Bridging the personal to the politically, we critically examine the intimate parts of our lives, histories, and experiences as sites of and for critical thought that inform acts of resistance by insisting on a politics of refusal. Taking an interdisciplinary approach and engaging with a diverse set of texts and creative forms of expression, we also explore the erotic as a method of inquiry and theoretical framework to understand how embodied knowledge might inspire new forms of connectivity and resistance. Students will engage with different forms of critical creative expression to foster an embodied understanding of the material discussed throughout the course.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Students will critically engage with theories of the erotic, examine its role as a transformative source of creativity and resistance, and apply their understanding to various sociopolitical contexts.
• Students will explore how the erotic serves as a practice of social and bodily awareness, emphasizing the connection between personal experience and intersecting dominant power structures.
• Students will develop an interdisciplinary framework for understanding the erotic as a source of knowledge for social critique and enacting social change.
• Students will cultivate writing skills and artistic practice to further develop their critical thinking.

course_name: Topics in Latina and Latino Studies of Space and Place

course_info.course_name: Topics in Latina and Latino Studies of Space and Place

course_details.Overview of class: This course is a mix of history and journalism that aims to help students interested in both approaches tell more complicated, fuller, richer, more accurate stories about Latinos in the United States—a population that is too often seen as immigrants or voters. You will read work by the best Latino journalists working today and discuss how to incorporate a historical perspective. Your final project will be to report and write your own story on Latinos in Chicago or anywhere else you choose.

course_details.Overview of class: This seminar provides students with the opportunity to reflect on their academic journey as students of Latina and Latino Studies. It is designed for those seeking an opportunity to conduct independent research and work in a collaborative writing workshop setting. In consultation with the professor, students will identify a general topic or subject for a research project at the beginning of the quarter relevant to the field of Latinx studies. Students can revisit ideas or papers from previous coursework or develop a new project. Approved student projects will shape the organization and structure of this course — such as course materials that we will consider together for discussion and feedback. The research and writing salon offers students practical guidance on developing research strategies and refining their project essays through writing exercises, work-in-progress workshops, and in-class writing time. Take note that prior coursework in Latinx Studies is required to enroll in this class.

Department consent required.

Prior coursework in Latinx Studies is required to enroll in this class. LATINO 201, LATINO 202, and/or LATINO 203, or approval by the instructor based on other coursework in Latina and Latino Studies
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Develop a research agenda and craft arguments that connect scholarship and show the evolution of a topic relevant to Latina, Latino, and Latinx Studies.
• Refine strategies for searching for, obtaining, and evaluating primary and relevant secondary source materials.
• Experiment with writing voice through assignments and in-class exercises that will help further develop the skills of synthesis, analysis, and the overall presentation of ideas.
• Practice providing constructive and generative feedback and addressing comments and suggestions received through the exercise of revision.
